title: Copenhagen: KB Hall, Montmartre Club and Armstrong's draw
summary: Anders recalls George Lewis's band opening the Montmartre, comparing crowds with Stan Getz and Louis Armstrong.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: What club did you play in in Denmark, did you tell?
Well you have to ask him. I know that we had so much time, I had time to look for the name of the place, I would ask for the name of the place every night.

Well actually the whole band did a concert in Copenhagen's largest hall, the KB Hall, which was very successful. It was so successful as a matter of fact that even though George planned to go back to the States after the Copenhagen venues, we talked him into staying and opening a new club that was there, the Montmartre Club. You opened the Montmartre Club, George did? Yeah, George opened it. The first band in there. The very first band in there. And I think that I've never seen so many people in my life, it was hard to get the musicians in there. And there was hundreds and hundreds of people standing outside waiting all night to get there. It was very, very crowded. We all had, at that time the dressing room wasn't finished yet, and we all had to stand in the kitchen during the intervals. Yeah, that's right. We had some beers and some fun out there. It was hard to cook though. You didn't get much of a chance to cook.
Well what band has drawn the best in Copenhagen of all the bands you've had in the Montmartre?

George's band, in the Montmartre, if you want to refer to that particular place. Yeah, that particular place. Yes. I mean George's band was outstanding. I haven't seen anything like it in the traditional field. Speaking about progressive and modern jazz, when Stan Getz and Moe's Allison opened the club, just after George and the band were there, there was a lot of people too.
So would you say Stan Getz and Moe's Allison at Drew George?

Well that's very hard to say because George was there for about I think eight or ten days in total, you know. And that was full, the club was full, very, every night. And Stan was there for almost a year. And the first eight days was very full naturally as it would be. And then it balanced out so that it was Friday, Saturday and Sunday was very full. And Copenhagen is a city of about a million people or something like that. And there's just a natural demand for jazz. And they stayed so long. Sure should have liked to have George playing there. But he came back and played there later on the second term.
So then George Louis Armstrong is about as well as anybody in Europe then, roughly.

I would say so. I mean Louis Armstrong is, I mean Louis Armstrong takes in a lot of people that are not particularly interested in jazz but because of the outstanding amount of publicity he gets and because he also plays humorous versions of numbers that are well known to a lot of old timers because you might realize that in Europe it's the young people that go for jazz, college students and all the young boys and girls. And Louis Armstrong was just the first band to come over and make a success out of jazz in Europe and he'll never be forgotten for that. So I mean he's a top drawer.
He draws better than George Louis.

He draws better than anybody. I mean he draws better than most classical singers or anything. I think he made ten concerts in the KB Hall last time he was there and that holds about four thousand people and that means that forty thousand people out of Copenhagen came to see him, you know. And that was just a year after he was there last time and it goes like that every time between forty and sixty thousand people and that's outstanding. I don't think there's a single entertainer in the whole world that can do that. And then it's not important what group Louis brings, you know. They don't even list the other musicians where they advertise Louis because I mean it's just him they want to see.
Do you ever have big bands in the Café Montmartre?

We can't. It's impossible. The acoustic is, you know, the room is just too small to feature a big band. I think about various occasions, jam sessions, there may have been ten or twelve musicians playing at a time, but that's it.
